# Executive summary 

The global economy is continuing to shake off the effects of its worst recession since the end of World War II.  The concerted efforts of governments and central banks around the world have successfully stabilised the financial system and prevented the recession from developing into a depression.  However, as far as copper demand is concerned the recovery has not been universal with demand recovering at a much faster pace in the developing economies compared with the world’s mature economies.  During 2009 demand in the developing economies increased by 7.2% to 11.9Mt while consumption in the mature economies declined by 21.8% to ~5.4Mt.  Overall we forecast that global refined copper consumption will increase by 5.4% this year to 18.2Mt.  During the forecast period refined consumption will increase by 3.4% p.a. between 2010 and 2025.  Demand will rise from 17.3Mt at the end of 2009 to 29.6Mt in 2025. 

We now expect base case mine production _capability_ to increase by 4.8% during 2010, to ~16.7Mt, by 4.9% in 2011, to ~17.6Mt, and by 3.5% in 2012 to ~18.2Mt.   In 2013 mine production capability is expected to be relatively unchanged at ~18.2Mt.  However, based on current plans, the general trend in base case mine production capability is for a steady decline from 2014 onwards as output is lost, either to mine closures, or grade attrition exceeding committed incremental expansion or committed new base case project capacity.  During the forecast period the greatest loss in mine production capability will occur in Latin America, followed by Asia, North America, Oceania, Africa and Europe.  China is the only region where mine production capability is expected to increase during the forecast period. 

Overall base case mine production capability is forecast to decline by 2% p.a. between 2010 (inclusive) and 2025 with output falling from a peak of ~18.2Mt in 2012 to ~11.5Mt in 2025.  However, note that this rate of decline excludes our mine disruption allowance (5% of initial mine production capability forecast) and any price related/market adjustment.  At the same time, demand for additional mine production (including the disruption allowance) to meet increased market requirements for refined metal will create an implied shortfall in mine output of ~0.3Mt/a in 2011, 3.4Mt/a in 2015, 8.1Mt/a in 2020 and 14.4Mt/a by 2025. 

We now expect base case global copper smelter production capability to increase by 8.6% this year, to 15.3Mt, relative to production in 2009 and by 8.7% in both 2011 and 2012 to 16.6Mt and 18.1Mt respectively.  The largest rise in 2010 will be

seen in China with the commissioning of Baoding (200kt/a) and Liangshan (100kt/a) smelters plus several smelter expansions. 

Base case global copper refined production capability is now expected to reach 20Mt in 2010 (+9.4%), 22.2Mt/a in 2011 (+10.7%) and 23.9Mt/a in 2012 (+7.8%).  However, the strength of growth in refined production capability is forecast to slow markedly from 2014 onwards and negative growth is expected from 2017 onwards.  As a consequence global refined production capability will increase by only 1.5% p.a. between 2009 and 2025.  However, in tonnage terms this equates to an increase of ~4.9Mt with global refined production capability reaching 23.2Mt in 2025. 

We have raised our global market surplus since our last quarterly report and now forecast that supply will outweigh demand by ~325kt.  Previously we expected a market surplus of 269kt.  Despite the increase, our surplus forecast is down markedly from last year’s surplus of just over 1Mt and reflects restricted supply growth (+1.2%) and robust (+5.4%) demand growth (though from a low base).  Demand outside of China is forecast to grow by 3.3% this year, therefore the 5.4% gain in global demand this year reflects ongoing strong demand growth in China (+9%).  China’s healthy rate of gain will reflect ongoing investment within the power sector, continued government subsidies, albeit at slightly lower levels and the beginning of recovery in export demand for copper containing goods.  Reflecting the much reduced market surplus prices are forecast to average $7160/t/t ($3.25/lb) this year, up 38.5% from last year’s average of $5170/t ($2.34/lb).

# 2009 in Review 

## Demand analysis 

**Global copper demand fell sharply last year** Towards the latter part of last year the global economy continued to shake off the effects of its worst recession since the end of World War II.  The concerted efforts of governments and central banks around the world successfully stabilised the financial system and prevented the recession from developing into a depression.  However, in terms of copper demand the damage had already been done, especially outside of China.  Since the end of Q1 last year we have lowered our 2009 demand estimates (excluding China) by a net 1.1Mt to ~10.8Mt (see table below).  Nevertheless, the sharp downturn was offset by a significant uplift (+1.3Mt) in our 2009 estimate of Chinese demand from the end of Q1 last year to now.  As a consequence of the Chinese revisions we have increased our 2009 global refined copper consumption estimate by a net 0.2Mt, to 17.3Mt, since the end of Q1 last year. Overall we estimate that global refined copper consumption decreased by 4% last year to 17.3Mt, the largest annual decline since 1982. 

**Western European demand particularly weak last year** The downward revisions we made to our Western European 2009 estimate reflected weakenin

g demand in Germany, Italy and France.  In all three cases demand last year continued to be hampered by the ongoing slowdown in the region’s construction sector.  This was particularly true of Italy where the country’s copper sector is heavily reliant on demand from the construction sector.  The extent of the downturn in Italy was highlighted by figures reported by Assomet, the country’s non ferrous national association, which showed that the production of copper bars and sections, sheet, strips and discs and tube fell by a combined 17.6% last year to ~123kt. The Association reported that the production of copper semi products, which included both copper and copper alloy products, fell by 20.6% last year to 937kt.  This was considerably below the more normal annual level of 1.3Mt. Reflecting this we forecast that Italian refined copper demand fell by 22% last year to just under 500kt.  Elsewhere in France, demand for copper was severely hampered by the closure of Nexan’s Chauny wire rod plant.  Originally the plant was earmarked for closure at the beginning of this year because of falling demand and over capacity.  However, the plant was forced to close in September because of industrial action which broke out following the company’s announcement of the forthcoming closures.  The plant never reopened.  As a consequence we estimate that French refined copper consumption declined by 43.3% last year to 215kt.  For Western Europe as a whole demand fell by an estimated 21.5% to ~2.7Mt. 

**Slow activity within the US construction sector continued to hamper demand** Demand for copper in the US was also hampered by slow construction activity last year.  This was highlighted by government statistics which showed a 29.5% decline in the number of housing completions from a year earlier.  Reflecting this copper wire rod production, according to the American Bureau of Metal Statistics, fell by ~23% (-335kt) to ~1.2Mt.  The Association also reported a 28% (-44kt) decline in wire rod imports last year which underlined the extent of the drop in demand even further.  Overall apparent demand, according to the ABMS, declined by 24.5% (-36.6kt).  Thus we estimate that US refined copper consumption fell by 21.2% last year to just over 1.5Mt.

**Japanese demand

weaker in 2009** Japanese demand for copper also fell sharply last year, reflecting weak demand from both the construction and auto sectors.  According to government statistics housing starts declined by ~28% to just over 788k units while total auto production fell by 32% to 7.9M units.  Reflecting this the Japanese Electric Wire and Cable Makers Association reported a 20.5% decline in shipments last year to their lowest level since 1975.  Shipments to the construction and automotive sectors fell by 18.3% (-63kt) and 31% (-28.5kt) respectively.  Reflecting this we estimate that Japanese refined copper consumption fell by 26.2% in 2009 to just below 900kt.

**Russian demand for copper impacted by change in cathode trade policy** In contrast, the significant decline in Russian refined copper consumption last year reflected a change in trade policy rather than the general global economic malaise.  Previously the Russians produced excessive amounts of copper wire rod for the export market to avoid the 10% duty on cathode exports.  However, in April last year the duty was abolished and, as a result, domestic copper producers preferred to export their cathode rather than convert it into wire rod.  This was highlighted by trade data for last year which showed a substantial 150.4% jump in exports to 508.9kt.  At the same time refined production totalled 838kt, implying that apparent consumption declined by ~52% to 329kt. 

**Strong Chinese demand in 2009** Finally, Chinese copper demand was supported by several factors in 2009, namely a boom in the construction sector, helped by an increase in the availability of credit, ongoing investment within the power sector and the introduction of government incentive schemes in both the auto and home appliance sectors.  The success of the government subsidy schemes was highlighted by Chinese auto production increasing by 47.7% last year, to ~13.8M units, while the production of electrical home appliances increased from H2 onwards.  According to China’s National Bureau of Statistics the output of air conditioner units fell by 20% year on year during H1.  However, for 2009 as a whole production was down by just 1.9% from a year earlier.  The increase in domestic demand for home appliances helped offset falling demand from overseas markets.  Another factor supporting Chinese refined copper demand last year was limited availability of copper scrap.  We estimate that the direct use of scrap consumed by semi manufacturers decreased by 20% last year due to a fall in imports (-28.5%), because of lower industrial activity within the developed economies.  Thus semi manufacturers were forced to purchase refined metal as their raw material source.  As a consequence we estimate that Chinese demand for refined copper increased by 27.8% in 2009 to 6.5Mt. 

## Supply Analysis 

###### **Mine Production** 

**Mine production increas

ed by 2.5% in 2009** During 2009 estimated global copper mine production totalled 16Mt of which 79% was derived from operations using conventional milling and flotation and the remaining 19% from the leaching of ores to produce SxEw cathode copper. Mine production increased by 2.5% from 2008’s level of 15.6Mt. **Net loss in copper mine production at its lowest in five years** Preliminary data suggests that the overall net loss in copper mine production last year, relative to initial expectations, was at its lowest level in over five years at just 3.3% (550kt Cu). This net figure comprises disruption losses of 4.8% (7.9% in 2008), closures of 2.2% (0.6%) offset by higherthan-expected output amounting to 3.7% (1.0%). It does seem the case that many equipment manufacturers and suppliers are now much better placed to meet demand within this sector. In addition, assuming that copper prices do not plummet to the levels seen in Q4 2008 there are unlikely to be any unexpected pricerelated closures in 2010. Thus, for 2010 we have taken a rolling five-year average for disrupted output and net pr

oduction gains, which is equivalent to a net 5% loss compared with 6% which had been assumed previously in our projections. 

###### **Smelter Production** 

**Small decline in global smelter production** Global smelter production of copper in blister and anode was 14.1mt in 2009 including 12.2Mt from primary sources and 1.9Mt from the reprocessing of scrap and repurchased blister.  Over 50% of primary smelter production is derived from custom concentrates (i.e purchased by smelters from third party mines) with the balance consumed in integrated facilities.  Compared with 2008 global smelter production fell by 0.8% last year.  This reflected production cuts due to concentrate shortages or difficulties in selling acid where smelters in Brazil, Canada, China, Finland, Japan and Sweden were affected. 

**Sharp rise in Chinese smelter production capability** Despite the market difficulties, Chinese smelter production capability increased by 10.2% last year to just under 3.2Mt.  This meant that China, for the sixth consecutive year, was the largest producer of smelted copper with a market share of 23%.  In 2008 China’s share was 20%.  The rise in smelted production reflected significant increases in production from the Dongying (+77kt), Guixi (+108kt), Jinchuan (+89kt), Jinlong (+48kt) and Shandong Xiangguang (+68kt) smelters. 

###### **Refinery Production** 

**Global refined production totalled 18.3Mt** Refined copper is derived form three sources; blister/anode from concentrates consumed at smelters, SxEw cathode for mines, and scrap (which is recovered at the smelting as blister/anode and at the refining stage as cathode).  In 2009 we estimate that global refined production amounted to 18.3Mt including 13.7Mt from concentrates, 1.3Mt from scrap and 3.3Mt from SxEw.  This was down by just 0.2% from 2008 where global refined production equalled just under 18.4Mt. 

**China remained the largest producer of refined copper** China, for the fourth consecutive year, was the largest producer last year with a global market share of 22.4%, up from 20.9% in 2008.  The next largest producer in 2009 was Chile, with a market share of 17.8%, followed by Japan (7.9%) and the USA (6.6%).  Countries comprising the former Eastern Bloc accounted for 33.3% of the overall market. 

**Two new refineries in China** China’s growth in market share last year reflected an increase of 274kt in refined production capability.  Part of the increase reflected two new refineries which came on stream.  These were the Fuwang (Yushan) (200kt/a) and Jiangxi Jinhui (100kt/a) refineries.  Between them they lifted refined capability by ~70kt. Elsewhere the uplift in capability reflected expanded production at existing refineries.  The most notable of these being Baoding (Dawufeng) (+70kt), Guixi (+98kt), Jinchuan (+89kt), Jinlong (+48kt) and Shandong Xiangguang (+72kt). 

## Market balances and prices 

**Disconnect between fundamentals and prices** The disconnect between copper prices

and market fundamentals widened last year, especially during the final quarter. This was underlined by official quotes reaching pre-crisis levels during November despite exchange inventories rising to their highest level in almost six years, weaker physical premia in most consuming regions, and China, where demand is strongest, remaining awash with metal. Prices averaged $6640/t in Q4 overall which was up 69% from Q4 2008 average of $3930/t. Metal stocks, in days consumption, rose from 45 days (in Q4 2008) to 69 days in the final quarter of last year. For the year as a whole prices averaged $5170/t ($2.34/lb) while supply outweighed demand by a massive 1Mt. **Large build in Chinese stocks** One of the key reasons for this disconnect related to the specific location of metal stocks. We estimate that Chinese cathode stocks increased by 0.7Mt by year end. In terms of days of global consumption, Chinese refined copper stocks, excluding SHFE inventories, finished 2009 at the equivalent of 25 days. And while Chinese stocks more than doubled from their previous typical levels of 16 days, there was only a modest uplift in stocks elsewhere. This was a key factor in the sense that the general feel of the market was one of little change in terms of stocks whereas, in reality, both the build up and displacement of inventories into less visible Chinese locations was significant. Going forward it is almost impossible to know when Chinese speculators may decide to release their copper metal inventories as each will have differing financial circumstances, purchase prices and selling price objectives. **Premia strengthen on Chinese demand** The strength of Chinese demand for cathode last year, which rose by 27.8% to 6.5Mt, led to stronger premia in areas where demand was not particularly strong. This was particularly the case with Europe where both grade A and Chilean material rose from just $20/t at the beginning of 2009 to a peak $83/t in May. The stronger level reflected material being shipped to China where higher premia could be achieved. By the year end European premia had eased to $55/t which was still strong in light of the region’s demand for copper. Meanwhile in Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - March 2010 Page 7 of 50 Copper Long-term Outlook China Shanghai premia reached a peak of $155/t in April before slipping to $60/t in December. The steady decline reflected the build up of stocks following record imports. Chinese net imports rose by 129% (~1.8Mt) last year. However, as far as copper demand is concerned the recovery has not been universal with demand recovering at a much faster pace in the developing economies compared with the world’s mature economies. Demand will rise from 17.3Mt at the end of 2009 to 29.6Mt in 2025. **Moderate recovery in mature economy copper demand forecast this year** As we have noted in previous reports 2010 will be a transitional year with demand increasing more strongly in 2011. Historically, strong first use copper demand growth has occurred 18 months to two years after the low-point in a recession-driven downturn in consumption. This is because many applications for copper in, for example, the construction sector, tend to be required towards the end of construction projects (plumbing, wiring, decorative items). Reflecting this, demand in the mature economies is forecast to recover by 1.6% this year, to just over 5.5Mt, before increasing by a more robust 4.7% in 2011 to ~5.8Mt. Thereafter, demand is expected to decline on an annual basis throughout the forecast period to 2025. As we noted in our previous Long Term Outlook report the negative trend reflects the displacement of first-use demand away from the mature economies to the developing economies, especially in China, Mexico, and Vietnam. In recent years there has been a growing trend of copper semis manufacturers moving their production facilities to areas where production costs (labour, environmental, power etc) are considerably lower. Prime examples include Mexico and Vietnam where two of China’s largest copper tube producers have recently set up new copper tube mills: Golden Dragon in Mexico and Hailiang in Vietnam. In addition, increased exports of competitively priced copper products from China, and other developing economies, into the mature economies will impact negatively on the production of copper semi products (from the mature economies) resulting in some production facilities becoming obsolete. This has already occurred within the wire rod market following the closure of Freeport’s Chicago plant at the end of 2008 an

d the more recent (September 2009) closure of Nexan’s Chauny wire rod plant in France.  Added to this one other European wire rod plant is rumoured to be facing imminent closure.  We now forecast that first-use demand in the mature economies will decline by 2.3% p.a. during the forecast period, falling from ~5.4Mt at the end of 2009 to ~3.7Mt in 2025

**Robust growth forecast in copper demand in the developing economies** Demand within the developing economies is forecast to grow by 7.2% this year, to ~12.7Mt, followed by further growth of 7.5% and 5.7% in 2011 and 2012 to 13.7Mt and 14.5Mt respectively.  The strong growth rates largely reflect robust Chinese demand which is expected to increase by 9% this year, 8% in 2011 and 5% in 2012 to ~7.1Mt, 7.7Mt and 8.1Mt respectively.  Further out, demand will continue to improve on an annual basis where refined copper consumption within the developing economies is forecast to increase by 4.9% p.a. between 2010 (inclusive) and 2025.  Thus refined copper consumption will rise from ~12Mt at the end of 2009 to 25.9Mt by 2025.  Strong growth in emerging economies will be supported by continued investment within the power sector. 

## China 

**Chinese economic growth remains firm** Chinese economic growth remains incredibly robust despite some key economic indicators having moderated from the highs reached last year.  Fixed Asset Investment (FAI) in the first two months of the year increased by 26.6% year on year.  While this was down from the 35%+ growth recorded during mid-

2009, it was very much in line with the 27% average of the past five years.  Also encouraging, in terms of future copper demand, was data which showed a 29.3% increase in floor space under construction during the first two months of the year from the corresponding period in 2009.  Housing starts, meanwhile, rose by a stronger 37.5% year on year over the same two-month period.  Growth within the construction sector is expected to remain strong through the year where copper demand will be supported by construction projects, which were star

ted in 2009 and are now moving towards completion.  Elsewhere demand will be supported by ongoing healthy growth in infrastructure investment and continued government fiscal stimulus measures. 

**Chinese demand forecast to increase by 9% this year** In 2010 we forecast that Chinese refined copper consumption will grow by 9% to ~7.1Mt.  At the beginning of the year there was concern that the announcement from China’s State Grid, which stated that the company will reduce its investment in electricity networks this year by 25%, would have a negative impact on demand in 2010.  However, we believe that the effect of the reduced spending will be limited.  This is because some of the investment made last year has not been used in 2009 and, therefore, will be carried into this year. This was confirmed by our sources who informed us that major wire and cable producers continue to report healthy order books and demand from the national power projects remains firm.  In addition, any negative impact from the lower investment will be partly offset by rising demand from the auto and home appliance sectors.  Most consumer appliance manufacturers in China are currently running at full capacity and report virtually full order books during H1.  Another encouraging fact is that there is typically a 6-12 month time lag between rising property sales and consumers’ purchases of home appliance products.  Therefore the strong recovery in the Chinese construction sector from June last year will bode well for future cathode demand. 

**Government subsidy programme for home appliances remains supportive** The success of the government subsidy programme for home electrical appliances continued to be highlighted by data from the National Bureau of Statistics. The Association reported robust growth in the production of refrigerators (+45.8%), washing machines (+47.5%), freezers (+33.7%), air conditioners (+27.7%) and computers (+41.1%) during the first two months of the year from the corresponding period in 2009.  During the first two months of last year production for all these products, barring washing machines and freezers, declined on an annual basis.  The continued increase in demand for these items will help support demand for copper and copper alloy products which is forecast to grow by 8.5% this year to just under 8.2Mt. 

**Export demand for copper intensive products expected to recover in 2010** It is possible that the strength of growth in demand for these copper intensive products will not be maintained throughout the year as the government acts to unwind some of the impact of their stimulus measures.  However, the gradual recovery of export demand for Chinese copper-intensive goods will counteract the negative impact that this will have on copper demand.  This was underlined recently by one copper plate and strip producer who reported that he expected demand to increase during the industry’s peak season in March and April because of healthy order levels from bot

h the domestic and export markets. The strength of demand was re-confirmed by a copper tube producer who announced that during February his plant operated at full capacity and orders during March were also strong. **Robust growth in Chinese copper demand this year** In 2011 we forecast that the dissipation of the impact of the government’s stimulus packages and last year’s surge in lending will be more than offset by strong demand for Chinese exports which will lift Chinese copper consumption by a further 8% to ~7.7Mt. Throughout the forecast period Chinese refined copper consumption is forecast to grow by 5.6% p.a., rising from ~6.5Mt at the end of 2009 to 15.5Mt by 2025. **French demand exceptionally weak** In France demand is exceptionally weak following the closure of Nexans 300kt/a Chauny wire rod plant last year.  The company’s Lens plant may take up some of this lost production following the plant’s announcement that it is aiming to increase capacity from 165kt/a to 190-195kt/a by adding an extra shift.  However, there have been problems with the casting furnace at the Lens plant because Nexans has preferred to increase the amount of scrap used rather than buy additional cathode.  According to our sources scrap material accounted for ~15% of the total furnace feed last year.  In addition to the problems associated with the furnace, the increased scrap intake will lower the quality of the rod produced.  Previously this would not have been a problem as the wire rod produced at the Lens plant was used to make energy cable which requires a lower grade of wire rod.  However, the Chauny plant produced a much higher grade of wire rod, as well as a greater variety, which will prove challenging for the Lens plant. New scrap, or manufacturing scrap, is generated during the fabrication of copper products and returned to the mill for reprocessing, or sold, and is not considered a new source of copper supply. A manufacturer may generate up to 60% of scrap as clippings, trimmings, stampings, borings, and turnings when processing copper and copper-base products into finished articles. New scrap is termed "run-around" or home scrap (which does not enter the scrap statistics) when it is generated internally at the plant re-using it, or it may be called "purchased return scrap" when returned by a customer from a plant external to that purchasing and re-using it. Old scrap is generated from worn out, discarded or obsolete copper products and thus, is considered to be a “new” source of supply ## Scrapping rates The availability of _old_ copper scrap is linked to the volume of copper-containing products installed/purchased and their life cycles, or duration. The life of copper in electrical equipment and machinery averages 30-35 years; in non-electrical machinery, 15 years; in housing, 35-75 years; in

transportation, 10 years; in all other sectors, about 10 years.  The average for the industry is estimated to be 15-20 years.  The rate of (old) scrap recovery and its availability to be the market is limited not only by copper's long life, but also by the sensitivity of scrap collection rates to market prices. 

Over the past 20 years, the volume of _new_ copper scrap has not grown in line with industrial consumption of copper because manufacturing efficiencies have improved, leading to as much as a 50% fall in new scrap generation over the period. 

## Scrap usage 

Most old scrap recovered from the market place must be reprocessed either by smelting and refining, or, to a lesser extent, by leaching and electrowinning to form a pure copper product.  Fire refining in a reverberatory or other furnace may be sufficient for the better grades of scrap.  This latter process uses oxidation, fluxing and reduction, with a refined ingot, wire bar, slab, or billet usually being the end product. 

Certain products, such as brass rod (manufactured using 80-90% scrap) can contain higher amounts of scrap than others while still maintaining product quality tolerance.  Others, such as wire rod, must contain far less impurities (typically 5%) since these could affect the drawability (leading to snapping) of the wire rod in producing wire.  New scrap is readily used by brass and copper tube mills to generate new semi-fabricated forms with little additional treatment. Because minimal clean-up procedures are needed, this type of scrap is commonly called "direct melt", or No.1 scrap.  In general, No. 1 scrap is contained in copper and copper-alloy products, rather than wire rod.  Scrap purchases by brass mills are based primarily on activity levels at the mills and the relative price differential between cathode and No. 1 scrap, rather than the actual copper price.  When business conditions are strong, brass mills have access to large volumes of return scrap.  When manufacturing (and, possibly imports) decline, mills may be forced to increase their cathode purchases. 

Low copper prices over the period 1997-2003 led to a reduction in the availability of smelting and refining grade scrap with a corresponding decline in the processing of this material in countries such the USA and in Europe.  The notable exception has been China where there has been an upward trend in the treatment of smelting and refining grade scrap material.  Economic and environmental considerations have also played a major role, with the cost of environmental compliance often leading to plant closures, particularly in the USA.  This is despite the fact that the cost of recovering one tonne of copper from scrap is approximately half that of recovery through the conventional route (concentratesmelting-refining).  Secondary smelters and ingot markers typically consume the lion's share (90%) of No.2 scrap and most of the auto radiators and red brass scrap.

If, as we believe, fund flows have amplified non-ferrous metals prices movements in recent history, they are likely to continue to do so in the future. The latter part of 2008 and early 2009 was characterised by the wholesale exit of investment funds from commodity markets; part of the flight to safety in the wider investment community. Extremely low bond yields and interest rates, coupled with high liquidity, have driven investors into leveraged plays like base metals, in the search for greater yield. The re-entry into base metals is seemingly predicated on a robust economic recovery, and as a result, the upside potential for prices has been diminished. As we transition out of the initial recovery phase, the temptation amongst investors must be to take profits and allocate them into asset classes that are better placed to produce a higher return than non-ferrous metals. We believe the most likely trigger for such a rotation out of commodities and into other asset classes would be a move by governments around the world to tighten monetary policy. India has already increased interest rates, China is facing inflationary pressures and the US and European Union will likely to look to increase rates from the second half of 2010. Curbing inflationary pressures through higher interest rates would increase the cost of leverage used by many investors and act as a drag on the pace of economic growth, reducing the attractiveness of base metals as an asset class. Such a development is likely to result in a slower pace of investor inflows into commodity markets during the latter part of 2010 and reduce the overall multiplier effect that these flows have had on prices. A reduction in the general level of inflows into non-ferrous metals markets is also likely to increase the chances of success of the investment strategies of the more specialist investors in non-ferrous metals markets. Potential strategies, such as shorting the aluminium and zinc markets, would have a greater chance of success

# Principle uses of copper 

Copper consumption can be divided into three main product groups which are copper wire rod, copper products and copper alloy products.  Copper wire rod, which accounts for an estimated 55% of total Global consumption (i.e. including scrap) and ~70% of primary consumption, is copper’s main first use.  With the exception of silver, copper has the highest electrical conductivity of all the metals.  This helps to explain why the principal application for copper wire rod is wire and cable.  Wire rod is consumed in five main wire and cable markets which include general and industrial cable, utility power cable, telecommunication cable, other insulated wire and winding wire. 

In general, wire and cable and copper products are consumed in five broad sectors: construction, electric and electronic products, industrial machinery and equipment, transportation equipment and consumer and general products.  Of these, construction is the largest sector for consuming copper, accounting for 33% of total copper consumption.  The main wire and cable and copper products consumed in the construction industry include building wire, power cable, copper plumbing and air conditioning tube, copper sheet and alloy products. 

Building wire is the largest of the wire and cable markets, accounting for ~35% of wire rod consumption.  Rising intensity of use, in both the mature and developing economies, will be largely responsible for building wire maintaining this position.  The number of electrical appliances used at home and at the workplace continues to rise, particularly in the mature economies, thereby leading to an increase in the number of power outlets needed per building.  In addition, recent technical issues imply that more copper wire and cable will

be needed in the future.  One of these issues, electrical energy efficiency involves using less power to perform a given task by using more or heavier copper conductors.  Finally, good power quality, defined as the uninterrupted, undistorted flow of electricity at the correct voltage, is also helping to drive up the demand for building wire due to higher power quality being achieved by installing additional circuits and heavier wires and cables. 

In contrast to the building and industrial cable market, the power utility market is the smallest of all the wire and cable segments.  However, demand growth for power cable will be supported by both the general recovery in utility investment and the fact that copper, the mainstay of power grids worldwide, still has considerable potential to carry energy better and reduce losses than aluminium. 

Copper tube, which accounts for an estimated 13% of global refined copper consumption, is the largest of the copper product markets.  The two main uses are in plumbing and heating systems and in air conditioners and refrigeration (ACR tube).  The steady proliferation of plumbing amenities in and around the home, particularly as many houses built today within the mature economies have more than one bathroom, are largely responsible for copper plumbing tube demand growth.  Elsewhere, improved living standards in the developing economies, leading to higher demand for air conditioners, continues to boost demand for ACR tube.  This is particularly the case in China and India where improved power supply will lead to a surge in the consumption of air conditioners over the coming years.  Meanwhile in the mature economies, the market is being driven by external factors such as environmental issues, regulatory concerns and social demands for comfort. 

Other copper and copper alloy products consumed by the construction sector include copper sheet and strip, rods, bars and sections plus brass products.  Copper sheet is used for roofing, eaves gutters, drain pipes for rainwater and lining for facades, while rods bars and sections, along with brass products, are used for building fixture and fittings.  In hospitals, brass doorknobs and push plates are widely used because it has been proven that they help to reduce cross contamination. 

Electrical and electronic products are copper’s second largest consuming sector, accounting for 33% of total copper demand.  Copper containing electrical and electronic products include telecommunication cable, power cable, transformer windings, semiconductors and motors for heavy appliances. 

Since the early 1990s copper telecommunication cable has been largely substituted by fibre optic cable in long distance networks.  However, owing to its high cost, copper telecom cable has remained the preferred link between the main network and consumers.  In addition, the development of the internet and e-mail has further enhanced the role of copper in telecommunications in recent years.  The need

for information to be carried quicker along the telecommunication network has led to the introduction of asymmetrical digital subscriber line technology (ADSL).  The ADSL is a dedicated circuit between a home and the telephone company’s central office that uses normal copper telephone lines.  The addition of an ADSL chip to the existing copper network means that users can download files around 15 times faster than an analogue dial-up connection. 

Dramatic gains in copper consumption to have occurred within the home because of a system known to the telecommunications industry as ‘structured wiring’.  The cable carrying voice, computer and television signals is connected to a central hub in the home.  Individual cables then run independently from here to high-quality connections in rooms throughout the house.  Cables connected to the hub consist of four pairs of twisted wires, capable of carrying more electronic signals with less interference and resistance than the older four-stranded telephone wires. ## Demand analysis 

The 2008 economic crisis that clearly affected metals demand globally could, in retrospect, have been detected in select consuming nations, such as the USA, as early as late-2007, and copper demand in the Western World at least contracted then by 1.7% to 12.1Mt.  On the whole, however, the more positive news of ongoing Chinese expansion carried the day, and globally copper demand increased by 3.1% that year, making it the second straight year of such growth rates.  Bearish tendencies held sway as we entered 2008 though, and by Q3 virtually all nations were beginning to detect the signs of a concerted slow down even if a complete awareness of the impending financial crisis had yet to dawn.  The collapse in the final quarter consumed everyone’s attention, and almost all data everywhere would point to a severe downturn in business levels, the likes of which we had not seen since the collection of comparable statistics began in the 1950s.  Western World copper demand fell again, therefore, but this time at almost double the rate of the prior year, at 3.4%, to 11.7Mt.  Even Chinese demand growth in 2008 of 9.2% year-on-year meant that, globally, copper demand declined marginally by 0.2% to ~18Mt. 

# China 

Chinese demand for copper increased by 9.2% in 2008, to 5.1Mt, which was only half the amount seen in 2007. However, in light of virtually zero global growth in 2008, this meant that China effectively too

k a higher proportion of global copper consumption than ever before, amounting to just over 28% - up 2% on the prior year. 

Final quarter Chinese data in 2008 implied that the country was indeed not immune to the collapse.  The country’s National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) reported that copper semis exports during Q4 2008 amounted to just 98kt, vs. 135kt for Q3 and 129kt for Q4 2007.  Equally, imports for Q4 2008 came to 187kt vs. 241kt for Q3 and 270kt for Q4 2007, implying quite a dramatic slowdown in Chinese industrial activity. 

# USA 

With the USA representing the start of the worldwide economic collapse during 2008, it is no surprise that copper demand there has continued its decline in terms of global importance. While we talk about the economic crisis of 2008, we can in fact trace the start of the downturn in US copper consumption all the way back to Q2 2006, when housing starts began their decline. In 2007 US refined copper consumption continued to be hampered by the downturn in residential construction activity which was more prolonged and much sharper than many had anticipated, especially following the eruption of the sub-prime credit crisis in that August. Even so, the ongoing strength in the automotive sector still allowed national copper demand to increase that year by almost 2.8% on 2006, to ~2.2Mt.  Indeed, it was not until late-Q1 2008 that the real spectre of a sustained decline in copper data became evident, as virtually all copperconsuming sectors could not withstand any longer the underlining message written by macro-economic collapse. 

As an example, from their peak of 128kt (metric - copper content) in March 2007, US brass mill shipments gradually tailed off over the course of the rest of that year, but still managed a reasonable 115kt in March 2008, according to data from the American Bureau of Statistics (ABMS).  A typically strong September (100kt) seemed to defy the odds for another month, but the typically low December tally of just 59kt adequately summarised the degree of exhaustion in the sector, and compared poorly with the previous year’s end performance of 86kt. 

Equally, we saw a parallel performance from the copper wire rod sector, where production plunged to 79kt (metric) in December 2008 vs. 99kt a year prior, according to the ABMS.  This brought the year on year decline to 8.4%, or 1.5Mt. Meanwhile, shipments of copper rod by US mills to domestic customers fell by 9% year on year to 1.5Mt (metric), fully one third lower than at the start of this decade. 

The poor market conditions brought even further contraction and rationalisation to the industry, following similar efforts in 2007.  Following on from the Q4 (2008) closure of FMI/PD’s 120kt Hawthorne rod mill near Chicago and three other companies which either closed or embarked on restructuring efforts at downstream facilities (such as winding/magnet wire), we expected that there would be some downtime, potentially further restructuring, ahead. # Copper Smelter Production 

Forecast individual smelter production levels are based on production **capability.** This is defined as the level of production that could reasonably be anticipated after allowing for normal disruptions.  Extraordinary factors such as labour strikes, major plant failure and other unpredictable events are not taken into account on a plant-specific basis until actually realised.  Individual production capability forecasts are based on planned output or set at a level that the smelter has demonstrably sustained.  This may be less than the official **capacity** of the plant.  No adjustments are made to individual smelter production capability forecasts as a consequence of forecast supply and demand imbalances until either an expansion or a cut in production (permanent or temporary) is confirmed.  When necessary a 'market-driven' adjustment is included in the overall supply and demand analysis.  If negative, this quantifies the amount by which global production capability must be reduced to match concentrate availability or, if positive, it represents the requirement for additional production that cannot yet be identified to individual projects. 

Global smelter production of copper in blister and anode was 14.2Mt in 2008 including 12Mt from primary sources and 2.2Mt from the reprocessing of scrap and purchased blister.  Over 50% of primary smelter production is derived from custom concentrates (i.e. purchased by smelters from third party mines) with the balance consumed in integrated facilities.  In 2008 China, for the fifth consecutive year, was the largest producer of smelted copper with a market share of 20.3%.  Previously Chile, with a market share of ~13% in 2003, had been the largest followed closely by Japan (~12%). 

According to historic precedent, and given sufficient concentrate feed, the primary copper smelting industry typically operates at an average rate of 87% of capacity.  Higher overall rates are rarely achieved due to a combination of planned and unplanned maintenance, strikes, restrictions on emissions, and in certain market conditions, lack of concentrates. 

Low copper prices over the period 1998-2003 led to a sharp reduction in copper mine output at a time when Chinese and Indian copper smelters were being expanded.  As a result, long-term treatment and refining charges (TC/RCs) declined significantly and spot rates even more dramatically to a point where many smelters could not justify participating in this latter market

# Copper Refinery Production 

Refined copper is derived from three sources; blister/anode from concentrates consumed at smelters, SxEw cathode from mines, and scrap (which is recovered at the smelting as blister/anode and at the refining stage as cathode).  In 2008 global refined production amounted to ~18.4Mt including 13.9Mt from concentrates, 1.5Mt from scrap and 3Mt from SxEw copper.  China is the largest producer of refined copper with a global market share of 20.9% in 2008, followed by Chile (16.7%), Japan (8.4%) and the USA (6.9%).  Countries comprising the former East Bloc accounted for 32% of the overall market. 

Output of electro-refined and fire-refined copper is critically dependent upon the availability of blister/anode from smelters and, to a far lesser extent, No.2 scrap.  The custom market for blister/anode copper is relatively small (<10%) and, given the highly integrated nature of the smelting/refining industry, changes in refinery capacity tend to occur in tandem with adjustments to smelting capacity. 

# Concentrates and Blister Markets 

###### Concentrates 

Unlike cathodes, there is no terminal market (e.g. the LME) for copper concentrates and pricing is thus established through a process of negotiation between buyer and seller.  A copper concentrate smelting contract is drawn up between the buyer and seller to provide a framework covering a whole range of terms and conditions.  These include a treatment and refining charge, price participation (pp) – if any, payables for copper, silver and gold, penalties for impurities (e.g. arsenic, bismuth, fluorine, etc), quotational periods for payable metals and payment terms that the miner (or trader) will pay to the smelter (or trader) for smelting and refining services.  The main aspects of the contract that are subject to negotiation are the treatment and refining charges (TC/RCs) that are expressed in US dollars per dry metric tonne of concentrate (the TC) and in cents per pound of payable copper (the RC) and (under long-term contracts) pp.  PP is a means whereby the buyer can participate in movements in the copper price above and often below agreed trigger prices. PP is usually expressed as a percentage (typically 10%) participation while there may only be one trigger price (e.g. 90c/lb) or two prices (e.g. above $1/lb and below 80c/lb). 

Long-term contracts can cover one year, or many years (typically up to thirteen) and may be evergreen in nature (i.e. they continue to operate indefinitely after the initial term has been concluded).  Most long-term contracts are renegotiated annually during the so-called Mating Season looking at a supply/demand balance of twelve months forward.  This typically commences in September, and can contin

ue through to April (or even later) the following year.  “Block” style contracts relate to 100% of the tonnage delivered during a calendar year while terms agreed under the more common “brick” pattern contracts apply to 50% of the following year and 50% to the year after and in this manner terms are established for 100% of the following year and 50% for the year after.  The concept of the brick contract is partly to attenuate the volatility of the market and partly to secure terms two years forward thereby reducing the risk of failing to reach agreement in non-holiday contracts. 

The custom concentrate market has been growing at an average rate of 4.9% p.a. since the mid-1990s while there has been virtually no net growth in the integrated sector.  During 2003 the size of the custom market exceeded that of the integrated sector for the first time.  In 2008 54% was sold to third parties, compared with 46% consumed in integrated facilities (i.e. almost the same as in 2007). 

Approximately 74% (75% in 2007) of custom concentrates were traded internationally in 2008 with the remainder sold to smelters within the same country.  Merchants captured 30% (29%) of the custom market and 16% (16%) of the overall market in 2008. 

Six countries comprise almost 80% of the internationally traded custom concentrate market.  While Japan’s was the major consumer of custom concentrates its dominance has been eroded, from almost 40% of internationally traded material in 1996, to 29% in 2003, and 25% during 2006 and 2007 and to 24% in 2008.  China’s significance in this market has risen steadily and is now larger than Japan, having more than trebled from just 8% in 1996, to 25% in 2008. India barely featured as a custom buyer in 1995, but rising domestic metal demand encouraged the construction of two large copper smelters that accounted for 11% of the international custom market.  South Korea’s share has been fairly stable at 8-10% post 1998 following a major smelter expansion.  Other participants, in descending order of significance, are Germany, Spain, Philippines and Bulgaria. 

During 2008 six copper producing countries accounted for approximately 75% of all internationally traded copper concentrates.  Chile’s dominance as the major custom concentrate supplier to the international market has been maintained for more than a decade although the country’s relatively constant market share of 40% declined during 2008 to 36% due to mine production disruptions, notably at Collahuasi and Escondida.

Custom copper concentrates are predominantly sold under long-term contracts with the remainder being available to the spot market.  The spot market differs from the long-term market in that virtually any tonnage can be offered for sale at any time of the year and there is normally no pp.  The seller contacts interested parties (usually traders) inviting them to submit bids t

o purchase the concentrate.  The seller will indicate the expected month(s) of shipment(s) and will ask the prospective buyers to submit their purchase terms.  Sometimes the seller stipulates most or all of these terms, leaving the buyer to offer just the TC/RC.  Spot treatment and refining charges are, therefore, determined through competitive bidding on a one-off, transparent basis.  Variations in spot terms tend to be much greater than in the long-term market which is to be expected given the high frequency of spot sales into an ever-changing market (low spot terms reflect a tight concentrate market and vice-versa).  Further given that the spot market reflects the marginal tonne of concentrate, in a deficit market traders will pay a premium (low TC/RC) for the material and in surplus years they will impose a discount (high TC/RC) on the material. 

Freeport (PTFI) and Mitsubishi Materials finally broke the stalemate between sellers and buyers in the 2009 concentrate Mating Season.  Just before Christmas (2008) the two sides fixed TC/RCs of $75/t & 7.5c/lb with no pp and a roll over of all other side terms.  These numbers were quickly adopted by most of PTFI’s other Japanese buyers (PPC is expected to formally accept these terms in February).  Having established this benchmark in Japan PTFI then went on to conclude deals in Chile, China, India, Indonesia, Korea, Philippines and Europe all at $75/t & 7.5c/lb.  In early January 2009 Escondida concluded deals with its Japanese counterparts, also at $75/t & 7.5c/lb with no pp and a roll over of other terms.  The Chilean miner then went on to settle other contracts in China, Europe, Korea and the Philippines. 

# Blister 

The size of the custom blister/anode market has been on the decline since the mid-1990s, having lost market share to the integrated sector.  This reflects an ongoing preference by many former custom blister/anode producers to add value at site, through brownfield expansion of existing refining capacity or greenfield development.  Over the 14-year period 1995-2008 the integrated sector grew by 4.7Mt and its market share rose from 86% to 91%. 

Within the custom sector sales to third parties within the same country comprise ~50% of this market with the balance sold internationally.  In absolute terms sales via traders have remained moderately flat over the 14-year period; merchants currently handle around one quarter of all custom blister/anode. 

In 2008 Belgium remained the major recipient of internationally traded blister/anodes with a market share of just under 25%.  These imports comprised purchases from custom suppliers and receipts from integrated smelting facilities in Bulgaria (Pirdop).  China also featured in this market (21%) as did the USA (15%) and Canada (11%).  Including Mexico and Korea these six countries consumed almost 80% of all internationally traded blister/anode.   China is likely to be the largest buyer of internationally traded blister from 2009 onwards. 

C

hile’s share of the internationally traded blister/anode market peaked in 2006 at almost 50%, but in 2008 fell back to below 40% which reflected a 30% decline in exports.  Bulgaria’s market share also grew prior to 2008, due to ongoing investments in the Pirdop smelter, although this is set to decline markedly post 2009 due to the start up of a new refinery at Pirdop during H2 2008.  Collectively, Chile, Bulgaria, DRC, Canada, Slovakia and Finland accounted for almost 80% of this market in 2008. 

## Market balances and prices 

Our copper price forecasts are developed from our assessment of the interaction of future supply and demand with an implicit assumption that prices will continue to behave in a cyclical manner, with the low point in each cycle largely determined by the cost structure of the industry.  Our Base Case mine, smelter and refinery data reflects the production intentions of existing producers plus any projects that are currently under construction or that are financed.  Assumptions are made about the level of “additional” production adjustments that are required to keep apparent metal stock levels within realistic limits seen through past price cycles.  These adjustments may be both positive and negative but no attempt is made to identify specifically the possible projects that could be developed in the longer term to meet a supply shortfall or existing operations that may be forced to close during periods of low prices. 

Copper prices were severely depressed for much of the period 1997-2003, with average 2002 quotes at their lowest level, measured in real terms, for over a century.  The initial catalyst for the downturn in prices was the Asian crisis that came about during 1997.  Subsequently the market had to contend with a severe US economic slowdown towards the end of 2000 that brought an end to one of the longest periods of US economic growth on record.  The impact of the US slowdown was accompanied by the implosion of the “I.T.” bubble in that country and elsewhere, leading to a particularly severe downturn in copper demand.  The US slowdown was felt across the globe with only one country, China, seemingly insulated from its effects.  The contraction in global copper demand, most notably in 2001 and 2002 and insufficient producer discipline in terms of reducing copper supplies prior to 2002, led to the accumulation of excessive metal inventories in exchange warehouses.  This situation was exacerbated by the relative strength of the US dollar

Additional supply was brought into production at a faster rate than was required by end users and so

metal stocks in exchange warehouses continued to build, reaching record levels.  At the end of 1997 inventories on the LME, Comex and Shanghai exchanges amounted to 458kt.  By April 2002 these had ballooned to an all time high of 1.5Mt before declining to 1.3Mt by year-end.  Over that period more than 3Mt/a of copper mine capacity had been either closed or curtailed.  At the same time, around 2.2Mt/a of greenfield and 2.4Mt/a of brownfield mine capacity was brought on stream, along with some of the curtailed mine capacity that was reactivated in response to weakening currencies against the US dollar. 

Another factor supporting high cost mine production at this time was extremely depressed treatment and refining charges in both the spot and long-term markets.  Charges were artificially depressed by the significant growth in custom smelting capacity in India and China at a time when concentrate supply was also growing, but at a slower rate.  Custom smelters in India enjoyed a significant tariff differential between imported concentrates and metal providing additional income to domestic custom smelters.  A VAT rebate scheme on Chinese copper concentrate imports plus a 2% tariff on domestic Chinese copper metal sales also provided smelters in that country with substantial additional income that was not available to custom smelters elsewhere in the world.  As a consequence, custom concentrate sellers enjoyed some of the lowest treatment and refining charges on record over this period. 

In response to ballooning metal exchange inventories further mine production cuts and other supply constraining initiatives were put in place during 2002 and 2003.  For its part, Codelco elected to curtail 100kt of its low-cost mine capacity in Chile in 2002 and then withhold 200kt of cathode from the market in 2003.  BHP Billiton suspended its 90kt/a Tintaya mine and cut output at Escondida by 345kt (160kt in 2002 and a further 185kt in 2003).  These initiatives proved very effective and copper prices rose substantially in late 2003 in tandem with rapidly declining exchange stocks.  These stocks fell by 487kt Cu during 2003 to finish the year at 806kt Cu.  At the same time average cash LME prices rose by 14.3%, compared with 2002, to $1779/t (81c/lb) in current terms. 

During 2004 global refined copper production increased by 4.3%, year on year, to just under 16Mt.  At the same time, refined copper consumption significantly outperformed the rise in supply with year-on-year growth of 9.4 % to ~17Mt, resulting in a global market deficit of around 1.1Mt Cu.  This abnormally high rate of consumption growth was in part due to robust economic growth and also due to a substantial consumer inventory correction (re-stocking).  This deficit was met in part by metal previously accumulated by Codelco (200kt), from the release of ~250kt from China’s strategic stocks and from metal exchange inventories which declined by 682kt during 2004. 

While there was a near-universal expec

tation that prices would decline in 2005 in response to rising supplies, particularly during the second half of 2005, the opposite occurred with cash quotes in the year rising by 28.4% to $3683/t ($1.67/lb). The surge in prices occurred in spite of falling global demand (down 0.3%) to ~179Mt, and rising refined production, up 4.1% to ~16.6Mt, which resulted in a global market deficit of ~390kt.  De-stocking, or downward inventory adjustment, was a major contributing factor to the decline in demand, particularly in the wake of the substantial replenishment of inventories that occurred in many regions during the first half of 2004.  Also reducing the requirement for primary metal was a reluctance by consumers to buy expensive cathodes which led to a marked rise in scrap consumption, particularly in China, and the substitution of copper in some markets brought about by high prices.  Smelter/refinery/SxEw production disruptions reduced metal supplies by around 770kt relative to initial expectations (600kt from smelters/refiners and 170kt from SxEw producers) which was somewhat higher than typical losses of ~500kt/a at that time.  Also fuelling the rise in copper prices in 2005 was the marked increase in ‘fund’ involvement where large amounts of money from so called ‘passive funds’ (i.e. insurance companies and pension funds) were directed into commodity index products and hybrid products. 

In 2006 average prices reached a new record of $6729/t ($3.05/lb) in current dollars.  The ~83% rise in price reflected healthy demand growth (+2.7%), in spite of seemingly lacklustre demand from China, and significant mine supply losses. We estimate that the tonnage of mine output lost during 2006 due to supply disruptions was 880kt, i.e. below the 1.06Mt of mine production lost in 2005.  The main contributors to these losses were limited ore availability at several producers (PTFI, Batu Hijau) and industrial action (La Caridad, Cananea, Escondida).  As a consequence total metal stocks (producer, consumer, merchant, transit and exchange) fell further during 2006 to just 39 days of consumption.  A normal level of stock is considered to be 60-65 days and hence overall stocks remained well below normal levels. 

In 2007 a further 950kt of mine production was lost through supply disruptions.  Despite these losses, the growth in refined production outweighed the 2.7% increase in refined consumption.  As a consequence inventories rose marginally, from 39 days of consumption in 2006 to 40 days in 2007.  This still represented critically low levels, and this was reflected in prices which increased from an average of $6729/t ($3.05.lb/) in 2006 to $7124/t ($3.23/lb) in terms. 

In 2008 overall stocks increased further, to 48 days of consumption.  The increase, in part, reflected the ongoing growth in refined production (+3.2%).  However, flat consumption year-on-year also contributed, and resulted in a global market surplus of ~415kt.
